   <guid>https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/19/musk-pledges-spacex-shares-to-every-us-child-in-potential-107bn-giveaway</guid>
   <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:35:58 +0200</pubDate>
   <description>Elon Musk says he will give one SpaceX share to every child in America next year, a pledge worth about $10.7bn (€9.5bn) at Friday’s closing price. He has yet to explain who would qualify or how the shares would be distributed.</description>

      <description><p>Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO</p><p>An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history kills more than 4,300 and sickens more than 9,000 people in the region.</p><p>It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries.       <title>LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/15/senegal-homosexuality-criminalised-anti-lgbtq-arrests-hiv-testing-human-rights-watch</link>
      <description><p>At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports</p><p>Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/10/12/senegal-brutal-crackdown-violates-lgbt-peoples-rights">new report</a>.</p><p>More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, <a href="https://www.hivjustice.net/cases/senegal-crackdown-on-lgbtq-people-intensifies-with-multiple-arrests/">according to HIV Justice Network</a>, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/15/senegal-homosexuality-criminalised-anti-lgbtq-arrests-hiv-testing-human-rights-watch">Continue reading...</a></description>

<rss version="2.0" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:media="http://search.yahoo.com/mrss/" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/"><channel><language>en</language><title>France 24 - International breaking news, top stories and headlines</title><description>Breaking news and world news from France 24 on Business, Sports, Culture. Video news. News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 15:09:33 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category></category><title>'Police weren't overwhelmed by people protesting and marching' about education and cost of living</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-police-weren-t-overwhelmed-by-people-protesting-and-marching-about-education-and-cost-of-living</link><description>
Oliver Farry is pleased to welcome Andrew Smith, Lecturer in Liberal Arts at Queen Mary University of London. France's escalating social unrest has exposed a troubling disconnect between legitimate popular grievances and the government's increasingly security-focused response. Smith argues that the violence accompanying otherwise largely peaceful demonstrations reveals serious failures of policing, while President Emmanuel Macron's response offers "very little of substance." Drawing parallels with France's historic protest movements, Smith identifies a "convergence of causes" rooted in economic insecurity, educational inequalities and political paralysis. He warns that a repressive response risks deepening the crisis, calling instead for a renewed commitment to "participatory social democracy."
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/bcf396a2-cbc5-11f1-9178-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261019-100920-101652-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/bcf396a2-cbc5-11f1-9178-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261019-100920-101652-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">c29781fe-cbc5-11f1-afb3-cd05e8c70964</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:58:36 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Four soldiers dead, dozens injured in fire at Canada military base</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-four-soldiers-dead-dozens-injured-in-fire-at-canada-military-base</link><description>
Four soldiers were killed and dozens injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta province, one of the worst peacetime tragedies to hit Canada's armed forces on home soil, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e49123dc-a087-11f1-8dc3-005056a97e36/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-08-24T163056Z-1186857443-RC2R3NAM318W-RTRMADP-3-CANADA-DEFENSE-ICEBREAKERS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e49123dc-a087-11f1-8dc3-005056a97e36/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-08-24T163056Z-1186857443-RC2R3NAM318W-RTRMADP-3-CANADA-DEFENSE-ICEBREAKERS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">1113910a-cbb3-11f1-9294-0daba255a691</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:25:09 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>French PM says 'ultra-left' seeking 'deep unrest' ahead of election</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-french-pm-says-ultra-left-seeking-deep-unrest-ahead-of-election</link><description>
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Monday accused the "ultra-left movement" of seeking to "orchestrate deep unrest across the country" in the runup to next year's presidential election. FRANCE 24 International Affairs Editor Angela Diffley looks back at Lecornu's remarks in the wake of the violent protests that shook the country over the weekend.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1b1526be-b330-11f1-abde-1d1125ed9143/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26142371784910.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1b1526be-b330-11f1-abde-1d1125ed9143/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26142371784910.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">240c10b8-cbc0-11f1-9076-f9791635338a</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:20:25 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Americas</category><title>Brazil court orders Meta to prove it gives Lula, Bolsonaro campaign content equal treatment</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261019-brazil-court-orders-meta-prove-gives-lula-bolsonaro-campaign-content-equal-treatment</link><description>

 
Brazil’s top electoral court has given Meta 24 hours to prove it is treating campaign content from incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro equally on its online platforms, threatening a daily fine for noncompliance. The ruling follows allegations from Lula's campaign that the social media giant is suppressing Lula’s campaign content ahead of Sunday’s closely contested presidential runoff.
 

 

 

</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/68cd318a-cb9a-11f1-b04b-638c1c1f5fd6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26292009828544.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/68cd318a-cb9a-11f1-b04b-638c1c1f5fd6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26292009828544.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">c3c284fa-cbc2-11f1-8230-6f7aedcd9302</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:16:05 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/68cd318a-cb9a-11f1-b04b-638c1c1f5fd6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26292009828544.jpg">© Andre Penner, AFP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>France protests draw global attention: Trump, Vance blame immigration for unrest</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-france-protests-draw-global-attention-trump-vance-blame-immigration-for-unrest</link><description>
US President Donald Trump on Sunday blamed immigration for unrest during protests in France and urged the country to tighten its migration rules. Trump's post comes after similar comments made by Vice President JD Vance on Saturday. Vance, who is seen as a potential presidential candidate in the 2028 election, also drew a connection to upcoming midterm races for congressional seats on November 3, where Republicans are not expected to perform well. FRANCE 24's Fraser Jackson reports from the United States.

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Mon, 19 Oct 2026 15:06:38 +0000 en <![CDATA[ 'They're kind of goth': NASA spacecraft gives mysterious brown dwarfs a close-up ]]> Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a host of "failed stars," also known as brown dwarfs.

These strange cosmic bodies straddle the line between planets and stars, possessing a mass between 13 and 80 times that of Jupiter (0.013 to 0.08 times the mass of the sun). They get the nickname failed stars because they form like stars from collapsing clouds of gas and dust but fail to gather enough mass to trigger the fusion of hydrogen to helium in their cores, the process that powers actual stars.

This formation process also means that brown dwarfs are cosmic loners, wandering the darkness of space alone, bereft of the light of a parent star. That description might sound like lyrics from a Type O Negative song ("Black No. 1," anybody?). And that's apt, according to the leader of the new study, which reveals that, chemically speaking, the atmospheres of these dark and cloudy worlds are not unlike those of our solar system's gas giant planets.

"They’re kind of goth," Zafar Rustamkulov, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Unlike exoplanets, free-floating brown dwarfs are completely independent celestial objects that will fade into eternity alone. We’re still learning how complex they are."

Rustamkulov added that, from Earth orbit, SPHEREx — short for Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer — sees wavelengths of light that are nigh-impossible to see with telescopes on the ground because water in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them. That is important for bringing brown dwarfs into the light.

"We are picking up light from the deep, red clouds of brown dwarfs all over the sky," he said.

A forest (of brown dwarfs)

Brown dwarfs have been somewhat mysterious since their discovery in the 1990s, due to the fact that the small amount of nuclear fusion that occurs within them causes them to emit no more than a faint glow. That means that our understanding of their makeup, their storms, and their evolution really only comes from theory.

To help lift this observational darkness, the team turned to data from SPHEREx. They studied 37 nearby brown dwarfs in a spectrum of light including 102 wavelengths, from the deepest red our eyes can see to the invisible infrared light. These local failed stars spanned the full temperature range for brown dwarfs — from 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 to minus 20 degrees Celsius).

Considering that the temperature of the sun is about 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit (5,500 degrees Celsius), you could definitely say brown dwarfs run cold.

The spectra of brown dwarfs seen by SPHEREx allowed the team to determine that their atmospheres are chemically rich in water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane.

"We’re seeing the signatures of these molecules and how they change from object to object across the entire temperature regime," said team member J. Davy Kirkpatrick, also of Caltech. "Our paper concentrated on just three dozen, but we have thousands more that we are in the process of analyzing.

"I really want to see what bounds the universe places on the variety of brown dwarfs."

All my colors

Brown dwarfs have been routinely observed by other telescopes, including NASA's James Webb Space Telescope and the agency's now-retired Spitzer Space Telescope, but the wide wavelength coverage of SPHEREx has made it particularly useful in observing these failed stars. That's good news for astronomers waiting for change in the atmospheres of brown dwarfs as they age and grow cold.

The researchers found that some brown dwarfs observed by SPHEREx are at a stage of extreme change in which their clouds are clearing, creating atmospheres rich in methane.

The team may have discovered significant new details about brown dwarfs, but they are still on the proverbial mystery street when it comes to these strange celestial objects,

"The state-of-the-art models are capturing the general chemical trend, but when it comes to these cloudy transitions, the models are struggling to match the data," said Rustamkulov. "No two brown dwarfs are alike. Even at the same temperature, their spectra look quite distinct."

"This journey has turned many of us into accidental meteorologists. We know how hard it is to predict weather on our own planet, and we realize it's going to be just as challenging to explain the phenomena we see in these bizarre, cold objects," Kirkpatrick said. "The findings are a call to action to explore even more of these dark worlds."

As astronomers resond to that call to action, I will ponder how I could have worked Bauhaus' Goth classic "Bela Lugosi is Dead" into this article.

The team's research was published on Sept. 28 in The Astrophysical Journal.

]]> <![CDATA[ Elephant Island is an icy sight from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 19, 2026 ]]>

Antarctica is a magnificent sight, and that beauty is visible all the way from space.

What is it?

Orbiting planet Earth, the European Space Agency's (ESA) Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission captured a close-up of West Antarctica.

Winter is ending in the Southern Hemisphere, meaning this is the peak of icy weather and sea ice in the Arctic.

In this image snapped by Sentinel-3, you can see a massive swath of ice which includes Elephant Island on the left-hand side. An ice-covered island off the Antarctic coast, Elephant Island floats in the Southern Ocean. It got its name both from the island's shape, which some liken to that of an elephant's head, and the fact that the island is home to a community of elephant seals.

Why is it incredible?

While a seal-inhabited island on the left floats near the Antarctic coast, across the water is a vast, frozen landscape. In just this snapshot, you can see about between 746 and 1,056 miles (1,200 to 1,700 kilometers) of the icy continent.

This image was captured on Sept. 30, 2026. In the Southern Hemisphere, that was just past the end of winter. The absolute peak for sea ice in Antarctica fell just a couple weeks before, on Sept. 14, according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center, ESA reported.

So in this one snapshot, we can see a near-maximum for sea ice in the Antarctic, spanning hundreds of miles. In observing our own planet from space, we are able to peer across vast landscapes, capturing important observational data. This is especially critical for the Antarctic as, with the progression of climate change, this sea ice continues to dwindle, adding to sea level rise among other serious consequences across the planet.

]]> <![CDATA[ Did a giant object collide with Earth to form the moon? ]]> For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon, pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms.

Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins, and how long has it orbited Earth?

Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours. Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today.

What do we know?

Birth of a lunar origin hypothesis

The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon.

Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours. Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets.

Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. Early in the following decade, the concept eventually claimed its place as the leading lunar-formation process during a landmark conference held in Kona, Hawaii, in 1984.

Evidence of a planetary-scale collision

The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario. For instance, researchers have long recognized the similar stable-isotope ratios between both moon rocks and those from Earth, strongly suggesting a link between their origins.

Additionally, the unusually high angular momentum (or spin) of the Earth-moon system, when compared to observations of other rocky planets, also could be explained as one of the effects of a massive collision.

Further clues can be found in the moon's composition, which reveals a relatively small iron core and lower density. This is significant to astronomers, since a hypothetical giant impact would have seen the suspected Theia protoplanet's metallic core merging with the young Earth's interior — meanwhile, lighter mantle and crust material from both worlds would have become dislodged and blasted into orbit, eventually helping form the moon.

Another important piece of evidence involves the relative depletion of volatile substances (a chemical that easily turns into gas or vapor at room temperatures) in lunar material, which again suggests that it might have been lost during an extremely energetic event, an idea further supported by evidence that the early moon once possessed a substantial magma ocean.

What remains unknown?

New research expands on the Theia hypothesis

Still, several significant questions remain, including what precise conditions led to the impact, and how the resulting planetary material evolved into the moon as it appears today.

Recently, a new study by Adeene Denton of Southwest Research Institute and colleagues at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory put a new spin on the Theia hypothesis, suggesting that the suspected ancient impact may have been significantly influenced by the heat and physical strength of the two colliding bodies.

The team's findings challenge some long-held views about the giant-impact hypothesis, while lending new support to others. For instance, the team's simulations revealed that while some impacts lead to the creation of a disk of debris that later coalesces into a moon, under other conditions, simulations support the idea that the moon could have been formed in a remarkably short period of time — perhaps within around five hours.

However, one of the primary issues with determining the exact conditions of the giant-impact hypothesis involves the ongoing debate over the moon's age.

"There is a large controversy regarding the age of the moon," said Dr. Erik Asphaug, a planetary science professor at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and one of the new study's co-authors.

In an email to Space, Asphaug explained some of the issues arising from this, since current estimates place the timing of the moon's formation anywhere from around 40 to 120 million years after the formation of the solar system. Therein lies part of the issue, according to Asphaug, who says this timing could have significant implications for models of the Theia impact.

If it had been an earlier collision, Asphaug says this would have involved a hotter Theia due to the greater degree of radiogenic heating; by contrast, a later impact would have meant a cooler and stronger Theia.

"I don't think we know enough yet to say the moon (and by corollary, the Earth) formed this way or that way," Asphaug told Space. "But knowing how temperature affects the result opens up a new dimension for viewing the problem, and that is always helpful because it shifts our frame of reference, like getting out of the car to have a walk around."

A lunar enigma in time and space

For researchers like Asphaug, understanding the moon's formation requires looking at it as more than just an event in space, but also as one in time. Doing so allows comparisons between three different metrics: isotopic decay, temperature-dependent material strength, and the geological record of debris striking other planets — a process through which he believes tighter constraints could be placed on precisely when the moon-forming impact might have occurred.

Adeene Denton, the study's lead author, also emphasized the introduction of the time component her team's research brings to the table, telling Space in an email that the outcome of the moon-forming impact could have depended significantly on the timing of the collision.

"Before, scientists have generally assumed that the outcome of the collision will be the same regardless of when it takes place," Denton wrote. "But now we know that temperature's effect on material properties, which is dictated by how old and/or cold the proto-Earth and Theia might be, alters things substantially."

]]> <![CDATA[ Watch Japan launch a bold sample-return mission to Mars moon Phobos today ]]>

Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time).

You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT).

As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars' two moons, Phobos and Deimos. They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km).

They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story.

The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement. (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.)

"Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added.

MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan.

The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029.

The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description.

"The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added.

The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world will scrutinize the Phobos sample for clues about the history and evolution of Mars and our solar system more broadly.

MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but issues with the H3 rocket prevented it from doing so. Mars and Earth align properly for interplanetary launches just once every 26 months, so MMX had to wait a while for its next chance.

Japan already has an impressive sample-return track record. The country's Hayabusa mission brought home pieces of the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, for example, and Hayabusa2 did the same with material from the space rock Ryugu a decade later.

]]> <![CDATA[ Returning the first samples from a Martian moon: Inside the science of Japan's bold MMX mission to Mars ]]> Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system.

The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago.

MMX is scheduled to launch on an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center on Monday (Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan, Oct. 20). After a 10-month journey to reach Mars, the spacecraft will spend about three years studying Phobos, deploying a rover and landing to collect its samples. The mission will then shift its focus to Deimos for a series of flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule is scheduled to land in Australia in 2031.

The spacecraft

The MMX spacecraft is comprised of three main parts, as well as a small rover. After release from its H3 launch vehicle, a propulsion module will provide the boost to put MMX on course for Mars. MMX's main exploration module carries the microwave-size IDEFIX rover and most of the mission's scientific instruments, while the return module houses the sample-return capsule.

Japan's Mitsubishi Electric built MMX's three main modules, with the French space agency CNES (Centre National d'Études Spatiales) and Germany's DLR (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft-und Raumfahrt) jointly developing IDEFIX. The little rover is named for a dog in the 1960s French comic "Asterix," in a nod to the country's first satellite, Astérix, which launched in 1965.

IDEFIX carries a suite of cameras, as well as the Raman Spectrometer for MMX (RAX) and miniaturized radiometer (miniRAD) instruments to analyze Phobos' surface composition and temperature.

Most of MMX's scientific instruments are housed on the exploration module, like NASA's Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL), and France's MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) instrument.

The exploration module also houses the Japanese-built TENGOO (TElescopic Nadir imager for GeOmOrphology) tight-zoom camera, wide-angle OROCHI (Optical RadiOmeter composed of CHromatic Imagers) multispectral camera, laser altimeter (LIDAR) and Mass Spectrum Analyzer (MSA). The return module, meanwhile, carries Japan's Circum-Martian Dust Monitor (CMDM) and Interplanetary Radiation Environment Monitor (IREM).

The mission

MMX will arrive in orbit around Mars in August 2027, at which point it will shed its propulsion module and transition into a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos that allows the probe to fly in a sort of formation with the small, asteroid-sized moon as they both circle the Red Planet.

The spacecraft will spend its first few months in the Martian system observing Phobos from different altitudes, using its TENGOO and OROCHI cameras, LIDAR and MSA to map the moon's surface, study its composition and select potential landing sites.

IDEFIX will be released in late 2028 or early 2029, during the first of two MMX landing rehearsals, at about 130 feet (40 meters) above Phobos. Due to the 14-mile-wide (22 kilometers) moon's extremely low gravity, the rover will be able free-fall to the surface damage-free (hopefully), right itself after a few bounces and begin exploring to gather data on the terrain and surface conditions.

MMX sample collection could begin as early as December 2028, the acting director of NASA's Planetary Science Division, Lindsay Hays, said during a mission briefing on Oct. 15. The spacecraft will attempt two collection landings, with its exploration and return modules descending and returning to orbit as one vehicle.

On Phobos' surface, two different sampling mechanisms — the Corer Sampling Mechanism (C-sampler) and Pneumatic Sampling Mechanism (P-sampler) — will extract and collect at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material for stowage inside the spacecraft's return capsule before MMX lifts off again for orbit. After its first touchdown and sample collection, MMX will return to QSO near Phobos before descending to a second landing site for a similar attempt and subsequent return to orbit.

MMX will end its observations of Phobos after about three years focused on the Martian moon, and will transition into a higher, resonant orbit around Mars in 2030. That course will repeatedly intersect Deimos' path for a series of flybys to collect and compare data with those from Phobos observations as scientists aim to investigate the moons' origins.

Near the end of 2030, the exploration module will separate, leaving the return module to fire its engine out of Mars' gravitational influence and begin an eight-month journey back to Earth with the collected samples. As MMX closes the last stretch of void during its approach to Earth in 2031, the sample-return capsule will separate and enter the atmosphere for a targeted parachute landing in Australia's Woomera region, where its contents will be recovered for laboratory analysis by Japan and its mission partners.

Phobos and Deimos

Those samples, and the data collected by MMX, could tell scientists a lot — about the moons' composition, geography and, perhaps most importantly, how they came to exist in the first place. There are two leading theories for Phobos and Deimos' origins, both of which point to very different versions of ancient Martian history.

"Phobos and Deimos are interesting, but not just in their own right. Their presence is a key piece of the larger story of the Mars system," said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and scientist in NASA's Planetary Science Division, during the Oct. 15 mission briefing. "By uncovering the moons' origin, we'll gain new insights into the history of both Mars and Earth, especially those events that shaped both planets billions of years ago and helped create the worlds we see today."

Both Phobos and Deimos are relatively small and irregularly shaped, and bear several resemblances and spectral characteristics to primitive D-type asteroids — ancient bodies thought to preserve material dating back to the solar system's formation about 4.6 billion years ago. Those similarities suggest Phobos and Deimos may have formed elsewhere in the solar system and were later captured by Mars' gravity.

Their near-circular, equatorially-aligned orbits around the Red Planet, however, somewhat complicate that theory. For example, a captured asteroid would be much more likely to have entered an elongated and tilted orbit akin to the direction and velocity of its original approach, scientists say. A competing hypothesis, therefore, offers a much more violent, but somewhat familiar, narrative for the moons' origins.

An enormous collision with ancient Mars could have blasted material into orbit to form a debris disk from which the two moons eventually coalesced. Such a process, which would be similar to the formation of Earth's moon, could explain their circular, equatorial orbits.

The contradicting geological and orbital observations for Phobos and Deimos collected to date have prevented scientists from definitively establishing one hypothesis over the other. MMX aims to provide an answer.

"It's two totally different lines of evidence that point in two different directions. That's what makes it an interesting puzzle," Statler said. Several theories have also been presented for hybrid scenarios combining the two, he added.

"There's all kinds of different ways, all kinds of different combinations of those two basic scenarios," Statler explained. "But that's the puzzle from the start, the two seemingly contradictory lines of evidence that are pointing us to what … the real history was, but we don't know what it is yet."

The science

Each theory for where Mars' moons came from predicts different chemical characteristics for their surfaces. Presumably, captured asteroids would preserve chemical signatures of material originating elsewhere in the solar system, potentially rich in volatile elements like hydrogen. Moons formed through a planetary impact, however, would contain a mixture of Mars and impact material, altered by the intense heat of such a violent collision.

Determining which scenario is more likely could reveal whether Mars experienced a massive moon-forming collision or acquired its moons from elsewhere in the early solar system. Either answer could offer new insights into the planet's evolution and the events that shaped the terrestrial planets like Earth billions of years ago, mission team members say.

"At this point, we know nothing about the composition of Phobos," David Lawrence, MEGANE principal investigator at APL, said during the Oct. 15 briefing. "We have information about mineralogy, but no elemental composition. And so, elements are really a key way to get at some of these foundational questions."

MMX's scientific suite has been carefully calibrated to make those determinations. The cameras and sensors on the MMX exploration module's TENGOO, OROCHI and LIDAR instruments will map Phobos' terrain, geological features and variations in surface materials from orbit, to provide clues about the moon's formation and evolution. Complementing those measurements, MIRS is designed to detect and classify Phobos' surface minerals and search for organic compounds to further differentiate its possible origin as an asteroid or ancient chunk of Mars.

The RAX spectrometer and miniRAD instrument aboard IDEFIX will add localized context to those observations by examining surface mineralogy and their thermal properties up close.

Back in orbit, NASA's MEGANE instrument will measure Phobos' elemental composition through gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy that can scan tens of centimeters beneath the moon's surface for signs of volatile elements. Higher abundances of hydrogen, chlorine, sodium and potassium, for instance, would favor the asteroid-capture hypothesis, while lower abundances of those compounds could point to the heat and chemical deterioration associated with a planetary impact.

"In Japanese, 'megane' means eyeglasses," Lawrence said. "So we like to think of MEGANE as being an instrument that will look at Phobos with gamma ray and neutron glasses."

When compared to the samples MMX will return to Earth, MEGANE's findings could help scientists determine if volatile depletion found on Phobos reflects the intense heat of a post-impact formation or billions of years of subsequent erosion from the natural effects of space exposure.

MSA, meanwhile, will measure charged particles around Phobos, searching for evidence of subsurface ice and investigating how solar wind exposure has altered the moon's surface. It will also study atmospheric particles escaping from Mars. CMDM will measure dust around Mars, including particles potentially ejected from its moons by impacts.

Comparative observations of Deimos after MMX's final departure from Phobos will help establish whether the moons share similar compositions and, potentially, a common origin.

Once safely returned to Earth, laboratory analysis of the Phobos samples will allow scientists to examine chemical composition and mineralogy with a precision beyond that of MMX's onboard instruments. Tests like isotopic analyses — measuring subtle differences in the atomic makeup of elements — can help identify the samples' origins by comparing their chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) scientists think some returned material could even originate from Mars itself, deposited on Phobos after ancient asteroid impacts blasted rocks off the Red Planet's surface, potentially holding evidence of its geological past.

International effort

The JAXA-led mission represents interagency partnerships with NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), which are providing hardware and communications support through the Deep Space and Estrack networks.

NASA's contributions to MMX also include MEGANE, the Honeybee Robotics-built P-sampler, and an approximately $87 million investment through the end of the mission. NASA is funding the United States scientists on the MMX team, who will, alongside NASA's astromaterials experts, "be fully involved in the examination and scientific analysis of the Phobos samples when they are delivered to Earth," Hays said during the mission briefing. "We get all of the value and all of the scientific participation at a lower cost total [than funding the entire mission]."

For its role, NASA will receive at least 15% of the returned samples, with materials to be maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation. To that end, MMX's scientific impact could extend far beyond the mission's conclusion.

"The Phobos samples will be historic," Statler said, with the potential "for future research to answer the questions we don't even know yet how to ask."

Those samples, and the data collected by MMX, could tell scientists a lot — about the moons' composition, geography and, perhaps most importantly, how they came to exist in the first place. There are two leading theories for Phobos and Deimos' origins, both of which point to very different versions of ancient Martian history.

"Phobos and Deimos are interesting, but not just in their own right. Their presence is a key piece of the larger story of the Mars system," said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and scientist in NASA's Planetary Science Division, during the Oct. 15 mission briefing. "By uncovering the moons' origin, we'll gain new insights into the history of both Mars and Earth, especially those events that shaped both planets billions of years ago and helped create the worlds we see today."

Both Phobos and Deimos are relatively small and irregularly shaped, and bear several resemblances and spectral characteristics to primitive D-type asteroids — ancient bodies thought to preserve material dating back to the solar system's formation about 4.6 billion years ago. Those similarities suggest Phobos and Deimos may have formed elsewhere in the solar system and were later captured by Mars' gravity.

Their near-circular, equatorially-aligned orbits around the Red Planet, however, somewhat complicate that theory. For example, a captured asteroid would be much more likely to have entered an elongated and tilted orbit akin to the direction and velocity of its original approach, scientists say. A competing hypothesis, therefore, offers a much more violent, but somewhat familiar, narrative for the moons' origins.

An enormous collision with ancient Mars could have blasted material into orbit to form a debris disk from which the two moons eventually coalesced. Such a process, which would be similar to the formation of Earth's moon, could explain their circular, equatorial orbits.

The contradicting geological and orbital observations for Phobos and Deimos collected to date have prevented scientists from definitively establishing one hypothesis over the other. MMX aims to provide an answer.

"It's two totally different lines of evidence that point in two different directions. That's what makes it an interesting puzzle," Statler said. Several theories have also been presented for hybrid scenarios combining the two, he added.

"There's all kinds of different ways, all kinds of different combinations of those two basic scenarios," Statler explained. "But that's the puzzle from the start, the two seemingly contradictory lines of evidence that are pointing us to what … the real history was, but we don't know what it is yet."

The science

Each theory for where Mars' moons came from predicts different chemical characteristics for their surfaces. Presumably, captured asteroids would preserve chemical signatures of material originating elsewhere in the solar system, potentially rich in volatile elements like hydrogen. Moons formed through a planetary impact, however, would contain a mixture of Mars and impact material, altered by the intense heat of such a violent collision.

Determining which scenario is more likely could reveal whether Mars experienced a massive moon-forming collision or acquired its moons from elsewhere in the early solar system. Either answer could offer new insights into the planet's evolution and the events that shaped the terrestrial planets like Earth billions of years ago, mission team members say.

"At this point, we know nothing about the composition of Phobos," David Lawrence, MEGANE principal investigator at APL, said during the Oct. 15 briefing. "We have information about mineralogy, but no elemental composition. And so, elements are really a key way to get at some of these foundational questions."

MMX's scientific suite has been carefully calibrated to make those determinations. The cameras and sensors on the MMX exploration module's TENGOO, OROCHI and LIDAR instruments will map Phobos' terrain, geological features and variations in surface materials from orbit, to provide clues about the moon's formation and evolution. Complementing those measurements, MIRS is designed to detect and classify Phobos' surface minerals and search for organic compounds to further differentiate its possible origin as an asteroid or ancient chunk of Mars.

The RAX spectrometer and miniRAD instrument aboard IDEFIX will add localized context to those observations by examining surface mineralogy and their thermal properties up close.

Back in orbit, NASA's MEGANE instrument will measure Phobos' elemental composition through gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy that can scan tens of centimeters beneath the moon's surface for signs of volatile elements. Higher abundances of hydrogen, chlorine, sodium and potassium, for instance, would favor the asteroid-capture hypothesis, while lower abundances of those compounds could point to the heat and chemical deterioration associated with a planetary impact.

"In Japanese, 'megane' means eyeglasses," Lawrence said. "So we like to think of MEGANE as being an instrument that will look at Phobos with gamma ray and neutron glasses."

When compared to the samples MMX will return to Earth, MEGANE's findings could help scientists determine if volatile depletion found on Phobos reflects the intense heat of a post-impact formation or billions of years of subsequent erosion from the natural effects of space exposure.

MSA, meanwhile, will measure charged particles around Phobos, searching for evidence of subsurface ice and investigating how solar wind exposure has altered the moon's surface. It will also study atmospheric particles escaping from Mars. CMDM will measure dust around Mars, including particles potentially ejected from its moons by impacts.

Comparative observations of Deimos after MMX's final departure from Phobos will help establish whether the moons share similar compositions and, potentially, a common origin.

Once safely returned to Earth, laboratory analysis of the Phobos samples will allow scientists to examine chemical composition and mineralogy with a precision beyond that of MMX's onboard instruments. Tests like isotopic analyses — measuring subtle differences in the atomic makeup of elements — can help identify the samples' origins by comparing their chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) scientists think some returned material could even originate from Mars itself, deposited on Phobos after ancient asteroid impacts blasted rocks off the Red Planet's surface, potentially holding evidence of its geological past.

International effort

The JAXA-led mission represents interagency partnerships with NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), which are providing hardware and communications support through the Deep Space and Estrack networks.

NASA's contributions to MMX also include MEGANE, the Honeybee Robotics-built P-sampler, and an approximately $87 million investment through the end of the mission. NASA is funding the United States scientists on the MMX team, who will, alongside NASA's astromaterials experts, "be fully involved in the examination and scientific analysis of the Phobos samples when they are delivered to Earth," Hays said during the mission briefing. "We get all of the value and all of the scientific participation at a lower cost total [than funding the entire mission]."

For its role, NASA will receive at least 15% of the returned samples, with materials to be maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation. To that end, MMX's scientific impact could extend far beyond the mission's conclusion.

"The Phobos samples will be historic," Statler said, with the potential "for future research to answer the questions we don't even know yet how to ask."

]]> <![CDATA[ Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton was a problem-solver for the ages (op-ed) ]]> Dean Robbins is a journalist and children's author. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights.

The pioneering computer scientist Margaret Hamilton, who died on Sept. 30 at age 90, played a key role in putting astronauts on the moon. She was a problem-solver extraordinaire, and it all started in early childhood.

Considering the name "daddy longlegs" unfair to female arachnids, young Margaret decided to call half of them "mommy longlegs." Wondering why the neighborhood baseball players were all boys, she determined to join the team herself.

As she grew up in the 1940s and '50s, Margaret noticed a similar problem with various professions. Why were doctors, judges and scientists almost always men? The solution: she would study hard in school and prepare herself for any job she might care to do.

It's no surprise that a born problem-solver would gravitate to computers. In the late 1950s, the new technology offered mind-bending possibilities, and this college math major saw a chance to put her skills to use on a cosmic scale.

Hamilton had long been a stargazer, thanks to a philosophical father who taught her to love the night sky. In 1965, after stints in meteorology and satellite tracking, she became interested in a Massachusetts Institute of Technology project that designed in-flight computers for NASA's moon mission.

The team, of course, consisted solely of men. But, just as with her neighborhood baseball team, Hamilton refused to accept limitations for herself or anybody else. She kicked open the door and quickly rose to director of software engineering.

With her knack for devising novel solutions to seemingly insoluble problems, no one was better suited for the job. Working with the era's primitive technology, Margaret thought through the various mishaps that could occur on a spaceflight and designed the software to handle every contingency.

The epochal Apollo 11 moon mission of 1969 put her planning to the test. As astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin neared the moon's surface in their lunar module, an error overloaded the onboard computer's processing unit. Mission Control faced the prospect of aborting the landing, but Margaret's ingenious programming allowed the system to prioritize essential tasks while canceling the inessential ones. The lunar module touched down without a hitch, and Armstrong and Aldrin became famous.

Sadly, Margaret Hamilton did not. She continued to work behind the scenes, contributing to the five additional lunar landings as well as Skylab and the space shuttle. In 1976, she struck off on her own to start a software company. She might have lived the rest of her life in obscurity if not for a fateful black-and-white photograph from 1969.

This image began to attract attention on the internet in the 2010s. It showed Margaret wedged between a coatrack and a blackboard at MIT, standing beside a towering stack of her printed code from the Apollo missions. Bespectacled and smiling, she radiates the confidence of a scientist who had stormed the boys' club and conquered the universe.

I was one of those fascinated by the photograph, and I contacted Margaret about the possibility of profiling her in a children's book. She initially resisted, uncomfortable with being the center of attention. But she came to see the appeal of a book about herself that she could read to her great-grandchildren, so that they might be inspired to break barriers themselves one day. She warmed to the task of telling her life story and even sent me examples of her Apollo code, which Lucy Knisley incorporated in the illustrations for "Margaret and the Moon: How Margaret Hamilton Saved the First Lunar Landing."

With the 2016 book and movie "Hidden Figures" calling attention to women's overlooked contributions to the space program, Hamilton soon had to get used to being the center of attention. She received a Presidential Medal of Freedom and achieved LEGO immortality in the "Women of NASA" set. In 2019, to mark the 50th anniversary of the first moon landing, Google used reflected moonlight to create a massive portrait of Margaret in the Mojave Desert. Rarely has so humble a soul received so grand a tribute.

The world will miss Margaret Hamilton, but, just like her great-grandchildren, we will always have her example to inspire us. She showed that, no matter how daunting the obstacles, there are few problems we can't solve.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Oct. 18, 1963: France's Félicette Becomes the 1st Cat in Space! >^..^< ]]>

On Oct. 18, 1963, a cat went to space! Félicette was a French "catstronaut" who became the first and only feline to fly to space.

While the U.S. and Soviet Union were busy launching primates, dogs and humans, the French decided to join the space race by launching a cat. Félicette, a stray tuxedo cat from the streets of Paris, was a substitute for another cat named Felix, who somehow escaped on launch day.

So Félicette went where no cat had ever gone before. She boarded a French Véronique AG1 rocket and soared 130 miles above the Earth before safely parachuting back down.

Luckily Félicette made it home alive and well, unlike many of the other animal astronauts that flew during the space race.

Why it mattered

Félicette survived spaceflight, but was short of this world. She was euthanized two months after her recovery so scientists could study her brain.

A second cat was launched by the French on Oct. 24, but its flight did not go so well, veering off course. When the cat was found a day later, it was discovered it have died as a result of the journey. From there on, CERMA (Centre d'Enseignement et de Recherches de Médecine Aéronautique) changed its research to flying monkeys.

Félicette may have become a footnote to history had it not been for a crowdfunded effort to raise a statue in her memory nearly 60 years later. The sculpture was unveiled in 2019 at the International Space University in Strasbourg, France. European astronauts Helen Sharman, Paolo Nespoli and Reinhold Ewald were on hand for its reveal.

In addition to the memorial statue, Félicette has been memorialized on postage stamps issued by Chad and Comoros, both former French colonies.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

]]> <![CDATA[ Astronomers want your help finding 'missing' black holes in the Milky Way ]]> Astronomers estimate that our home galaxy, the Milky Way, has churned out more than 10 million black holes over its 13-billion-year history. Yet so far, they have found only 70.

Now, a group of astronomers in the U.K. is trying to close that vast gap by enlisting the public. Their project, called Black Hole Hunters, is looking for volunteers with a computer and a few spare minutes to sift through troves of data gathered by a NASA space telescope. By flagging recognizable patterns that could point to a "missing" black hole, volunteers can help fast-track a search that would otherwise take years, the team says.

"You'll be narrowing down precisely where we need to point our telescopes next," project co-lead Adam McMaster, an astronomer at the University of Southampton in the U.K., said in a statement, "and you might be the one to discover a black hole."

Cosmic magnifying glasses

Black holes form when massive stars roughly 20 times heavier than our sun run out of fuel and collapse, leaving behind an abyss with gravity so immense that even light cannot escape. While invisible themselves, these cosmic behemoths reveal their presence by bending the light of nearby objects, and the Black Hole Hunters project is searching for one specific manifestation of this effect.

It happens thanks to the fact that massive stars often form in pairs, and a star can sometimes survive the violent supernova explosion that turns its companion into a black hole. When that happens, the two bodies continue to orbit each other. If such a duo aligns just right with Earth, the black hole will periodically pass directly between its companion star and our planet. And when it does, the black hole's gravity acts like a cosmic magnifying glass, bending and magnifying the star's light, causing it to briefly appear brighter to watchful telescopes.

To find these hidden giants, the project relies on data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, or TESS. Although the satellite's primary mission is to hunt for planets beyond our solar system, its method of data collection — tracking tiny, continuous changes in a star's brightness over time — is ideally suited for identifying black hole magnification events, the project description notes.

"It's a simple task with no expertise required," McMaster said in the statement. "We will show volunteers examples of what to look for so all they have to do is recognise the right patterns."

Automated algorithms conduct a preliminary sweep of the TESS data, screening millions of potential stars for the most obvious black hole candidate locations, according to the project description. But, the researchers say, artificial intelligence struggles with the messy realities of the cosmos, such as stellar flares and the natural pulsations of stars that can trick the algorithms into false positives.

The human touch

That makes human volunteers a key part of the search. To keep errors in check, each graph is shown to multiple volunteers, and their answers are combined so that individual mistakes average out, according to the project's website.

"I can search for black holes on my laptop from my bedroom — and could make a real impact on real space science," Grace Clarke, an undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the University of Southampton who's involved with the project, said in the same statement. "The data's easy to understand — it's just pattern recognition — and you don't need a degree in astronomy to read it."

The crowdsourced shortlist of promising signals lets astronomers aim follow-up observations at specific stars, such as precise measurements of whether a star is being tugged at by an unseen companion. Those measurements take time and are expensive, so a good shortlist helps researchers spend scarce telescope time wisely, the team says.

Since launching on the Zooniverse platform in October 2021, the project has attracted nearly 23,000 volunteers, who have completed more than 12 million classifications, according to its website.

Before turning to TESS, the team ran a similar search using data from SuperWASP, a ground-based survey that, like TESS, monitored stars for signs of planets from 2004 to 2016. Those results are still being analyzed and are expected to be published soon.

The team also plans to widen its search with observations from other instruments, including the European Space Agency's Euclid mission and NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

"With potentially thousands of new discoveries, we need all the help we can get," McMaster said in the statement.

]]> <![CDATA[ 10 best places to see the 2027 total solar eclipse in Spain ]]> Spain is one of the easiest places in the world to experience the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027. The so-called "eclipse of the century" first makes landfall in Andalucía, where totality will last up to 4 minutes and 40 seconds during mid-morning, with the sun comfortably high at around 38-42 degrees above the horizon in the eastern sky. Excellent roads, plentiful accommodation and Málaga's international airport make this an obvious alternative to North Africa and the Middle East.

However, choosing where to watch requires some thought. Southern Spain's narrowing shape funnels the path toward the Strait of Gibraltar, potentially concentrating huge numbers of eclipse chasers around Tarifa, the Costa del Sol and the British Overseas Territory of Gibraltar during the peak summer holiday season.

From busy Mediterranean beaches to mountain villages, here's where to see the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027 in southern Spain. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

1. Tarifa

Location: Cádiz province

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 40 seconds

Historical August cloud cover: 13%

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

At the southernmost tip of mainland Europe, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea, Tarifa is likely to be one of the country's busiest eclipse-watching locations because it will experience the longest totality in mainland Spain. Just 9 miles (14 km) across the Strait of Gibraltar from Morocco, the historic port town is known for its whitewashed old town, the medieval Castle of Guzmán el Bueno and its long, sandy beaches. Los Lances and Valdevaqueros offer wide horizons and plenty of open space.

2. Gaucín

Location: Málaga province, Andalucía, Spain

Start of totality and duration: 10:46 a.m. CEST; 3 minutes, 13 seconds

Historical August cloud cover: 5%

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

For eclipse chasers who would rather head into the mountains than join the crowds on the Costa del Sol, Gaucín is an intriguing alternative. One of Andalucía's classic pueblos blancos, the whitewashed village occupies a spectacular position in the mountains above the coast, crowned by the ruins of Castillo del Águila. Its elevated setting offers sweeping views across the surrounding countryside towards Gibraltar and, on clear days, the mountains of North Africa. Crucially, heading inland doesn't sacrifice too much totality.

3. Gibraltar

Location: Gibraltar

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 29 seconds

Historical August cloud cover: 17%

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

Few places in Europe could provide a more dramatic setting for totality than Gibraltar, the tiny British Overseas Territory dominated by its famous 1,398-foot (426-meter) limestone Rock. However, eclipse chasers will need to view either from The Rock or its east coast, where elevated viewpoints and beaches face the Mediterranean and the eclipsed sun. However, Gibraltar has a potential complication — the easterly Levanter wind can create a distinctive cap of cloud over the Rock even when surrounding skies are clear. Another issue is accommodation, which is already at a premium. See Gibraltar Eclipse 2027.

4. La Línea de la Concepción

Location: Cádiz province

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 24 seconds

Historical August cloud cover: 17%

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

Immediately north of Gibraltar, La Línea de la Concepción occupies the sandy isthmus between the Bay of Gibraltar and the Mediterranean Sea. Its location creates one of Spain's most distinctive possibilities for eclipse photography. On the Mediterranean side, Playa de Santa Bárbara is a wide sandy beach north of the border, with the immense Rock of Gibraltar rising to the south — a potentially spectacular foreground. The city has around 9 miles (14 kilometers) of coastline, providing plenty of alternatives for eclipse viewing.

5. Estepona

Location: Costa del Sol, Málaga province

Start of totality and duration: 10:46 a.m. CEST; 3 minutes, 41 seconds

Historical August cloud cover: 7%

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

About an hour's drive southwest of Málaga Airport, Estepona is one of the Costa del Sol's most attractive resort towns, with a pedestrianized old quarter of whitewashed streets, colorful flowerpots and squares centered on Plaza de las Flores. For eclipse day, the mile-long Playa de la Rada is the obvious gathering place, with its broad Mediterranean horizon and proximity to the town center. Other attractions include Estepona Marina and the Sierra Bermeja mountains rising behind the coast.

6. Cádiz

Location: Cádiz province

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 2 minutes, 56 seconds

Historical August cloud cover: 13%

Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east

Historic Cádiz occupies a narrow peninsula jutting into the Atlantic and is packed with reminders of its long maritime past, including the Cádiz Cathedral, the Roman Theatre and Torre Tavira, one of more than 100 watchtowers once used to spot approaching ships. For eclipse day, the long, sandy Playa de la Victoria offers plenty of open space, while La Caleta provides a more historic setting between two coastal castles.

7. Málaga

Location: Málaga province

Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 2 minutes

Historical August cloud cover: 9%

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Now, their efforts to bring the wonders of space exploration back down to Earth have earned them one of science communication's most prestigious honors: the Stephen Hawking Medal.

The honor recognizes all four crew members, including NASA astronaut Christina Koch, who wasn't in attendance.

For Wiseman, the experience of seeing our home planet from the vicinity of the moon carried a powerful message.

"If we could take each of you 250,000 miles away from this planet, 400,000 kilometers away from planet Earth, and you would see Earth the size of your thumb. It's tiny," Wiseman told the audience.

"When you're there looking through the moon, back at this tiny Earth, the only thing you feel is love, peace, hope, unity", he continued. "Those aren't the right words, but that is all you feel."

During their historic Artemis II mission, the astronauts did far more than put NASA's Orion spacecraft through its paces. Through live communications, interviews and glimpses into life aboard the spacecraft, not to mention the jaw-dropping photos that just keep on coming, they helped turn an extraordinarily complex mission into something people worldwide could experience and connect with.

And that's exactly what the Stephen Hawking Medal is designed to celebrate.

Established in 2016 by physicist Stephen Hawking and Starmus, the award honors those who have gone above and beyond to make science accessible, engaging and inspiring.

The Artemis II crew joins some pretty impressive company. Previous recipients include Apollo 11 moonwalker Buzz Aldrin, naturalist David Attenborough, primatologist Jane Goodall and astrophysicist Neil DeGrasse Tyson.

This year's ceremony marks the medal's 10th anniversary, with filmmaker Ridley Scott also among the 2026 honourees.

"It's a special thrill for us at Starmus to be able to honor the intrepid Artemis II crew members in the same way that we honored the Apollo astronauts who paved the way to the moon over 50 years ago," Starmus co-founder and Queen guitarist Brian May said in a statement ahead of the ceremony.

Wiseman left the audience with one final thought.

"When you come home to this beautiful planet, you realise that it's in every single one of us to choose to make tomorrow better," he said. "So let's all choose to make tomorrow better".

Starmus VIII runs from Oct. 17-22 across Tenerife and La Palma in the Canary Islands. This year's festival, themed "The Search for Truth", brings together leading scientists, astronauts, musicians and artists to celebrate scientific discovery and explore the importance of evidence and scientific thinking.

   <title>Itálie v šoku. Města demolují i děti, policii zasypaly doma vyrobenými bombami</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/evropa/protesty-italie-milan-deti-domaci-bomby/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=evropa</link>
   <description>Obyvatelé Itálie jsou zděšeni. Mnozí přestali kvůli víkendové vlně násilí a rabování vycházet ven. Opevňují se v bytech a čekají, co bude dál. Část země ovládly chaos, strach a panika. Policisté se stali lovnou zvěří násilníků a nestačí obnovit bezpečí v ulicích. Anonymní Hnutí 17. října přitom hrozí na sítích opakováním teroru každou sobotu až do doby, než padne vláda.</description>

  <item>
   <title>Znásilnění a vražda matky otřásly vesnicí na Plzeňsku. Lidé dodnes nezapomněli</title>
   <link>https://plzensky.denik.cz/krimi/pribehy-zla-plzensko-herbrych-vrah-matka-znasilneni-dozivoti-soudce-jan-speta-vzpominky-sousede/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=krimi</link>
   <description>Když se lidé v Sedlci u Starého Plzence na Plzeňsku dozvěděli, jak skončila jejich bezproblémová sousedka, 68letá Žofie Š., běhal jim mráz po zádech. Starou ženu totiž zavraždil a ještě předtím polomrtvou znásilnil její vlastní syn, kterého si k sobě vzala domů poté, co si odpykal trest za vraždu jiné, 83leté stařenky. O doživotním trestu rozhodl plzeňský soudce Jan Špeta, který na případ, jenž je dalším pokračováním Příběhů zla, pro Deník zavzpomínal, stejně jako někteří obyvatelé Starého Plzence.</description>
   <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
   <guid>https://plzensky.denik.cz/krimi/pribehy-zla-plzensko-herbrych-vrah-matka-znasilneni-dozivoti-soudce-jan-speta-vzpominky-sousede/</guid>

   <enclosure url="https://ceskolipsky.denik.cz/images/api/image/1366x768/1ae/1ae7cf9f-0b59-4513-b293-52627b533a68.jpeg" length="0" type="image/jpeg"/>
   <media:content url="https://ceskolipsky.denik.cz/images/api/image/1366x768/1ae/1ae7cf9f-0b59-4513-b293-52627b533a68.jpeg" medium="image" height="768" width="1366">
    <media:description>Soudce Krajského soudu v Plzni Jan Špeta, který uložil dvojnásobnému vrahovi Vladimíru Herbrychovi trest doživotí.</media:description>

  <item>
   <title>Žlučníkové kameny už se týkají každého desátého Čecha. Operace není vždy nutná</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/zdravotnictvi/zdravi-zlucnikove-kameny-priznaky-lecba-kdy-jit-na-operaci/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=zdravotnictvi</link>
   <description>Žlučníkové kameny se podle odborných odhadů týkají přibližně každého desátého Čecha. Ne všechny končí operací, které se navíc během let hojně posunuly. Dnes lékaři devadesát procent z nich provádějí laparoskopicky. Pomáhají jim i roboti. Zatímco dřív byli lidé po zákroku hospitalizováni týden či deset dnů, dnes obvykle jeden den.</description>
   <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 10:30:00 +0200</pubDate>

    <media:description>Odborníci odhadují, že žlučníkovými kameny trpí asi každý desátý dospělý člověk. Ilustrační foto</media:description>

  <item>
   <title>Ota Jirák přežil infarkt i mrtvici. S manželkou zachránili starou hospodu </title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/kultura/zemrel-ota-jiral-prezil-infarkt-i-mrtvici/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=kultura</link>
   <description>Na televizní obrazovce umíral už v první epizodě Slunečné, ve skutečnosti se dokázal vrátit do života po infarktu i mrtvici. Ota Jirák, který v neděli zemřel ve věku 77 let, byl mužem mnoha talentů. Herec, mim, dabér, ale také malíř, sběratel zbraní a zachránce staré venkovské hospody. Nejvíc se ovšem proslavil jako hlas dobrosrdečného chlupáče Heleho, k němuž se dostal tak trochu oklikou.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Zaměstnanci veřejné sféry si polepší, v průměru o čtyři tisíce na hlavu</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/jednani-o-rustu-platu-v-pristim-roce-odbory-cmkos-vlada.A261019_124530_domaci_kop#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Lidé, kteří pracují ve veřejné sféře, si od ledna významně polepší.  Zástupci vlády a odborů pokračovali v pondělí ve  vyjednávání o růstu platů ve veřejném sektoru pro příští rok. „Vyhlašuje se konec tarifů pod minimální mzdou,“ řekl ministr práce a sociálních věcí Aleš Juchelka z ANO k platům zaměstnanců veřejné sféry po jednání. Bude se to týkat několika set tisíc lidí.</description>
      <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 15:19:02 GMT</pubDate>
      <category domain="https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci">Zprávy - Domácí</category>

    <item>
      <title>Hlaváček znovu jednal s Piráty a Prahou sobě. O koalici se rozhodne do pátku</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/volby-koalice-praha-ods-stan-pirati-jednani-hlavacek.A261019_131536_volby_dyn#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>V Praze by mělo být během tohoto týdne jasno o složení vládnoucí koalice. Vítězný STAN se v pondělí znovu setkal se zástupci Pirátů a Prahy sobě, jednání s oběma stranami budou pokračovat ještě ve středu. O partnerství Starostů se SPOLU pro Prahu už nejsou pochybnosti, čeká se jen na to, zda strany vytvoří koalici samy, nebo s dalším partnerem. Rozhodnutí by mělo padnout ve čtvrtek.</description>
      <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 15:17:00 GMT</pubDate>
      <category domain="https://www.idnes.cz/volby">Zprávy - Volby</category>
      <comments>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/volby-koalice-praha-ods-stan-pirati-jednani-hlavacek.A261019_131536_volby_dyn/diskuse</comments>
      <guid isPermaLink="false">A261019_131536_volby_dyn</guid>
      <media:content url="https://1gr.cz/fotky/idnes/26/102/cl6/DYN8fcb92ed9a_163024_5546216.jpg" type="image/jpeg" />
      <media:description>V Praze pokračují jednání o složení vládnoucí koalice. Podruhé se lídr STAN Petr Hlaváček sešel se zástupci Pirátů, které vedla Tereza Nislerová (19. října 2026)</media:description>

      </media:group>

    <item>
      <title>Mladá Boleslav má jasno o koalici. Město dál povede primátor Bouška</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/praha/mlada-boleslav-volby-koalice-ano-stan-primator-bouska.A261019_162301_praha-zpravy_ichuc#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>V Mladé Boleslavi bude pokračovat dosavadní koalice ANO a Volby pro Mladou Boleslav, STAN, ODS s TOP 09 a Hlasu pro Boleslav. Čtyři uskupení mají v třiatřicetičlenném zastupitelstvu 25 mandátů. Primátorem zůstane Jiří Bouška z vítězného uskupení ANO a Volba pro Mladou Boleslav.</description>

    <item>
      <title>V deltě Nilu objevili hlavu kolosálního Ramesse II. Socha měla přes osm metrů</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/zahranicni/v-egypte-nasli-cast-sochy-faraona-ramesse-ii-giganticka-hlava-meri-1-6-metru.A261019_151711_zahranicni_pzak#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Významný archeologický nález se podařil v egyptské provincii Gharbíja v deltě Nilu. Zvláštního kamenného bloku si na svém pozemku všiml místní obyvatel a ohlásil ho úřadům. Archeologové pak na místě našli další části dávného uměleckého díla, především hlavu obrovské sochy jednoho z nejvýznamnějších faraonů Ramesse II. </description>

    <item>
      <title>PŘEHLEDNĚ: Deset příkladů sociální pomoci a podpor, které Francouzi mají, ale Češi ne</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/zahranicni/10-konkretnich-prikladu-socialni-pomoci-a-podpor-ktere-francouzi-maji-ale-cesi-ne.A261019_143413_zahranicni_remy#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Česká sociální síť je poměrně velkorysá, nicméně francouzský úřad CAF nabízí podporu, o které se tuzemským rodinám, studentům i pracujícím může jen zdát. Podívejte se na 10 příkladů sociální pomoci a finančních příspěvků, které Francouzi berou jako samozřejmost, ale v České republice neexistují.</description>

      <title>Bhútán nebo Mauritánie. Prezident Pavel přijal nové velvyslance</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/bhutan-nebo-mauritanie-prezident-pavel-prijal-nove-velvyslance.A261019_164555_domaci_kkos#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Petr Pavel převzal na Pražském hradě pověřovací listiny nových mimořádných a zplnomocněných velvyslanců. Ani jeden z nich nebude sídlit v Praze. Šlo o první oficiální bod prezidentova programu po jeho návratu z dvoutýdenní soukromé zahraniční cesty. Oficiální ceremoniál se však uskutečnil bez jakéhokoli Pavlova vyjádření nebo možnosti dotazů od médií.

      <title>Subway chce v Česku znovu růst. Po útlumu plánuje stovky nových restaurací</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/ekonomika/podniky/subway-navrat-pobocek.A261019_153436_ekoakcie_vebe#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Řetězec Subway se chce po útlumu v Česku znovu rozšířit. Z původních 21 restaurací zůstaly čtyři, další franšízanti své pobočky během covidu a po růstu cen energií zavřeli. Nový regionální master franšízant Emerging Bites nyní plánuje síť oživit. V pěti zemích střední Evropy chce během deseti let otevřít 300 restaurací.</description>

      <title>Zeman na Hrad na udílení vyznamenání nepřijde. Nemám rád gesta bez obsahu, řekl</title>

      <description>Bývalý prezident Miloš Zeman se 28. října opět nezúčastní slavnostního předávání státních vyznamenání na Pražském hradě u příležitosti výročí vzniku samostatného Československa. Místo toho zamíří na slavnostní shromáždění Českého svazu bojovníků za svobodu v Praze. Jeho předchůdce Václav Klaus na hradní ceremoniál dorazí.</description>

<item>
<title>Miton věří v AI agenty v e-commerce, miliony posílá do služby, která jim umožňuje hlídat ceny napříč trhem</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/miton-veri-v-ai-agenty-v-e-commerce-miliony-posila-do-sluzby-ktera-jim-umoznuje-hlidat-ceny-napric-trhem/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Dal&#353;í sázku na AI agenty v e-commerce vypsal Miton, který investuje do českého DeepScoutu, startupu, který právě otevírá svou databázi e-commerce dat umělé inteligenci. Ta je může využít k tvorbě vlastních cenových strategií, analýz a automatizací. Technologie DeepScoutu umí z e-shopů vytáhnout ceny, dostupnost i sortiment a poznat, které produkty si navzájem odpovídají. Doteď ji využívali hlavně velcí obchodníci včetně Alzy.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Iva Brejlová)</author>
<pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:27:57 GMT</pubDate>
<enclosure url="https://i.iinfo.cz/images/389/miton-a-deepscout.jpg" length='42832' type="image/jpeg"/>
<guid isPermaLink="false">www.lupa.cz-actuality-18632</guid>


</item>
<item>
<title>Český operátor spouští levnější konkurenci Applu či Googlu pro ukládání obrázků a dokumentů v cloudu</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/cesky-operator-spousti-levnejsi-konkurenci-applu-ci-googlu-pro-ukladani-obrazku-a-dokumentu-v-cloudu/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Český mobilní operátor O2 spou&#353;tí něco, co by &#353;lo nazvat konkurencí pro Apple iCloud, Google Drive a dal&#353;í podobné služby pro ukládání souborů v cloudu. Novinka se jmenuje O2 Můj Cloud a má fungovat jako osobní cloudové úloži&#353;tě.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Jan Sedlák)</author>
<pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 10:55:41 GMT</pubDate>
<enclosure url="https://i.iinfo.cz/images/398/o2-muj-cloud.png" length='19537' type="image/png"/>
<guid isPermaLink="false">www.lupa.cz-actuality-18629</guid>


</item>
<item>
<title>Albertu kvůli kyberútoku už déle než týden nefunguje aplikace, v zahraničí vypadly i rozvozy</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/albertu-kvuli-kyberutoku-uz-dele-nez-tyden-nefunguje-aplikace-v-zahranici-vypadly-i-rozvozy/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Obchodní řetězec Albert má už více než týden nefunkční mobilní aplikaci Můj Albert. Preventivně ji vypnul kvůli kybernetickému incidentu v mateřské skupině Ahold Delhaize a zatím stále není jasné, kdy se podaří ji zprovoznit.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Iva Brejlová)</author>
<pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 10:05:30 GMT</pubDate>

</item>
<item>
<title>Výrobce špičkových routerů a modemů z Vysočiny má rekordní tržby. Většinu vyváží do světa</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/vyrobce-spickovych-routeru-a-modemu-z-vysociny-ma-rekordni-trzby-vetsinu-vyvazi-do-sveta/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Česká republika má zavedeného výrobce moderních technologií pro bezdrátový přenos dat, takže se tento obor nesoustředí pouze do &#352;védska, Finska, USA nebo Číny. Společnost Racom z Nového Města na Moravě navrhuje a vyrábí rádiové modemy, mobilní routery a mikrovlnné spoje, často pro průmysl, kritickou infrastrukturu, SCADA systémy a podobně. V loňském roce dosáhla na rekordní čísla.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Jan Sedlák)</author>
